claim: Protein-protein interactions involving intrinsically disordered proteins are important for cellular function and common in all organisms.
source: Protein-protein interactions involving intrinsically disordered proteins are important for cellular function and common in all organisms.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about IDPs.

claim: CID appeared after the divergence of protostomes and deuterostomes 450–600 million years ago.
source: CID appeared after the divergence of protostomes and deuterostomes 450–600 million years ago, while NCBD was present in the protostome/deuterostome ancestor.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic reconstruction data presented in the manuscript.

claim: NCBD was present in the protostome/deuterostome ancestor.
source: CID appeared after the divergence of protostomes and deuterostomes 450–600 million years ago, while NCBD was present in the protostome/deuterostome ancestor.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic reconstruction data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The most ancient CID/NCBD formed a relatively weak complex (Kd∼5 µM).
source: The most ancient CID/NCBD formed a relatively weak complex (Kd∼5 µM).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: At the time of the first vertebrate-specific whole genome duplication, the affinity had increased (Kd∼200 nM).
source: At the time of the first vertebrate-specific whole genome duplication, the affinity had increased (Kd∼200 nM) and was maintained in further speciation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: The affinity of CID/NCBD was maintained in further speciation after the first vertebrate-specific whole genome duplication.
source: At the time of the first vertebrate-specific whole genome duplication, the affinity had increased (Kd∼200 nM) and was maintained in further speciation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: New interactions involving intrinsically disordered proteins may evolve via a low-affinity complex which is optimized by modulating direct interactions as well as dynamics.
source: Experiments together with molecular modeling using NMR chemical shifts suggest that new interactions involving intrinsically disordered proteins may evolve via a low-affinity complex which is optimized by modulating direct interactions as well as dynamics, while tolerating several potentially disruptive mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (NMR, ITC) and molecular modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Evolution of IDP interactions tolerates several potentially disruptive mutations.
source: Experiments together with molecular modeling using NMR chemical shifts suggest that new interactions involving intrinsically disordered proteins may evolve via a low-affinity complex which is optimized by modulating direct interactions as well as dynamics, while tolerating several potentially disruptive mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing similar affinities despite sequence variations.

claim: A substantial fraction of the proteome is made up by intrinsically disordered proteins.
source: While the majority of proteins fold into well-defined structures to function, a substantial fraction of the proteome is made up by intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) (Uversky and Dunker, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Uversky and Dunker, 2012.

claim: IDPs play pivotal roles in biology by participating in protein-protein interactions that govern key functions such as transcription and cell-cycle regulation.
source: These IDPs, which can be fully disordered or contain disordered regions of variable size, play pivotal roles in biology, usually by participating in protein-protein interactions that govern key functions such as transcription and cell-cycle regulation (Uversky et al., 2008; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Uversky et al., 2008 and Wright and Dyson, 2015.

claim: IDPs are present in all domains of life.
source: IDPs are present in all domains of life, but they are more common and have a unique profile in eukaryotes as compared to archea and bacteria (Peng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peng et al., 2015.

claim: IDPs are more common and have a unique profile in eukaryotes as compared to archea and bacteria.
source: IDPs are present in all domains of life, but they are more common and have a unique profile in eukaryotes as compared to archea and bacteria (Peng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peng et al., 2015.

claim: IDPs appear to evolve faster than structured proteins.
source: One particular problem with analyzing structure-function relationships in IDPs with regard to evolution is that IDPs appear to evolve faster than structured proteins and are more permissive to substitutions that do not apparently modulate function in either a positive or negative way (Brown et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2011.

claim: IDPs are more permissive to substitutions that do not apparently modulate function.
source: One particular problem with analyzing structure-function relationships in IDPs with regard to evolution is that IDPs appear to evolve faster than structured proteins and are more permissive to substitutions that do not apparently modulate function in either a positive or negative way (Brown et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2011.

claim: Insertion and deletion of amino acids are more common in IDPs.
source: In addition, insertion and deletion of amino acids are more common in IDPs (Brown et al., 2010; Light et al., 2013), further complicating structure-function analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2010 and Light et al., 2013.

claim: The two paralogs CREBBP and p300 likely result from whole genome duplications.
source: The two paralogs CREBBP and p300, as well as the three paralogs NCOA1, 2 and 3, likely result from whole genome duplications.
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analysis and established knowledge of vertebrate genome duplications.

claim: The three paralogs NCOA1, 2 and 3 likely result from whole genome duplications.
source: The two paralogs CREBBP and p300, as well as the three paralogs NCOA1, 2 and 3, likely result from whole genome duplications.
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analysis and established knowledge of vertebrate genome duplications.

claim: The ancestral vertebrate(s) went through two rounds of whole genome duplications (1R and 2R) prior to the origin of jawed vertebrates.
source: The general conclusion is that the ancestral vertebrate(s) went through two rounds of whole genome duplications (denoted 1R and 2R, respectively) prior to the origin of jawed vertebrates, and that teleost (bony) fish experienced a third whole genome duplication (3R) (Hughes and Liberles, 2008; Van de Peer et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hughes and Liberles, 2008 and Van de Peer et al., 2009.

claim: Teleost (bony) fish experienced a third whole genome duplication (3R).
source: The general conclusion is that the ancestral vertebrate(s) went through two rounds of whole genome duplications (denoted 1R and 2R, respectively) prior to the origin of jawed vertebrates, and that teleost (bony) fish experienced a third whole genome duplication (3R) (Hughes and Liberles, 2008; Van de Peer et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hughes and Liberles, 2008 and Van de Peer et al., 2009.

claim: Genomic duplications are beneficial for inventing new biochemical functions.
source: Genomic duplications are beneficial for inventing new biochemical functions (Ohno, 1970; Näsvall et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ohno, 1970 and Näsvall et al., 2012.

claim: NCBD is older than CID.
source: This analysis shows that NCBD is older than CID, as NCBD can be traced in deuterostomes, protostomes (including extant arthropods, nematodes and molluscs) and cnidarians, but not in more distantly related eukaryotes such as the choanoflagellate Monosiga brevicollis.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: NCBD can be traced in deuterostomes, protostomes and cnidarians.
source: This analysis shows that NCBD is older than CID, as NCBD can be traced in deuterostomes, protostomes (including extant arthropods, nematodes and molluscs) and cnidarians, but not in more distantly related eukaryotes such as the choanoflagellate Monosiga brevicollis.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: NCBD arose in the animal lineage as a domain within the ancestral CREBBP/p300 protein.
source: Hence, NCBD arose in the animal lineage as a domain within the ancestral CREBBP/p300 protein.
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analysis showing NCBD presence in animals but not in more distantly related eukaryotes.

claim: CID appeared as an IDP domain within NCOA after the split of deuterostomes and protostomes.
source: CID, on the other hand, appeared as an IDP domain within NCOA after the split of deuterostomes and protostomes, since it could not be identified in protostome NCOA.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing CID absence in protostomes.

claim: CID was present in an early deuterostome before the first whole-genome duplication (1R).
source: Furthermore, CID was present in an early deuterostome, before the first whole-genome duplication (1R), since it could be traced in extant sea urchins and acorn worms, in addition to vertebrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing CID presence in sea urchins and acorn worms.

claim: The CID/NCBD interaction emerged at the beginning of the deuterostome lineage around the Cambrian period.
source: Thus, we conclude that the CID/NCBD interaction emerged at the beginning of the deuterostome lineage around the Cambrian period, an era with a very dramatic evolutionary history.
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analysis and inference about when the two domains first co-existed.

claim: The affinity of deuterostome/protostome (D/P) NCBD for 1R CID was relatively low (5 µM) as compared to younger NCBD variants.
source: Strikingly, the affinity of deuterostome/protostome (D/P) NCBD for 1R CID, which is the oldest CID domain that we were able to resurrect with good confidence, was relatively low (5 µM) as compared to younger NCBD variants (Figure 5A and B, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: All tested ancestral D/P NCBD variants measured with 1R CID yielded a relatively low affinity (Kd values = 1.5 to 18 µM).
source: Importantly, all tested ancestral D/P NCBD (Thr2062) variants measured with 1R CID yielded a relatively low affinity (Kd values = 1.5 to 18 µM).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: Around the time of the two vertebrate-specific whole genome duplications (1R and 2R), NCBD had evolved an affinity toward the CID domain similar to that found today (∼200 nM).
source: Already around the time of the two vertebrate-specific whole genome duplications (1R and 2R, respectively), NCBD had evolved an affinity toward the CID domain similar to that found today (∼200 nM).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: All tested alternative variants of 1R/2R NCBD, 1R CID and 2R CID yielded Kd values in the same range (100–300 nM).
source: All tested alternative variants of 1R/2R NCBD, 1R CID and 2R CID yielded Kd values in the same range (100–300 nM) (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in Table 1.

claim: The affinities between extant NCBD domains and human CID domains were found to be surprisingly similar across several species.
source: Moreover, the affinities between extant NCBD domains and human CID domains were found to be surprisingly similar across several species.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: CREBBP NCBD from sea lamprey and human have similar affinity toward human NCOA3 CID.
source: For example, CREBBP NCBD from sea lamprey and human, respectively, has similar affinity toward human NCOA3 CID.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: The affinities of p53TAD and PNT for ancient and extant NCBD were similar.
source: In contrast to the CID domain, the affinities of p53TAD and PNT, respectively, were similar for ancient and extant NCBD (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in Table 1.

claim: The NCOA3 CID domain from human displays a high degree of disorder.
source: The NCOA3 CID domain from human displays a high degree of disorder (Ebert et al., 2008; Kjaergaard et al., 2010b) and all tested CID variants in the present study displayed a strikingly similar far-UV CD spectrum, typical of IDPs (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ebert et al., 2008 and Kjaergaard et al., 2010b, as well as CD data in Figure 7.

claim: All tested CID variants displayed a strikingly similar far-UV CD spectrum, typical of IDPs.
source: The NCOA3 CID domain from human displays a high degree of disorder (Ebert et al., 2008; Kjaergaard et al., 2010b) and all tested CID variants in the present study displayed a strikingly similar far-UV CD spectrum, typical of IDPs (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: The overall α-helical propensity for ancient and modern CID variants is virtually identical.
source: The similar shape and midpoints of the resulting sigmoidal curves (reflecting the helix-coil transition) demonstrates that the overall α-helical propensity for ancient and modern CID variants is virtually identical.
evidence: This claim is supported by TFE titration experiments reported in Figure 5C and Table 2.

claim: The stability for individual α-helices as predicted by AGADIR has changed during evolution.
source: We note, however, that the stability for individual α-helices as predicted by the software AGADIR (Muñoz and Serrano, 1994) has changed during evolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational predictions using AGADIR software.

claim: α-helix 1 of CID from human NCOA1 and 2 displays a higher α-helix propensity than α-helix 1 from human NCOA3 and the ancestral versions.
source: For example, α-helix 1 of CID from human NCOA1 and 2 displays a higher α-helix propensity than α-helix 1 from human NCOA3 and the ancestral versions (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by AGADIR predictions shown in Figure 8.

claim: Extant mammalian CREBBP NCBD has a small but well-defined hydrophobic core.
source: While extant mammalian CREBBP NCBD has a small but well-defined hydrophobic core, it is a very dynamic protein domain in the absence of a bound CID domain as previously shown by NMR measurements (Ebert et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ebert et al., 2008.

claim: NCBD is a very dynamic protein domain in the absence of a bound CID domain.
source: While extant mammalian CREBBP NCBD has a small but well-defined hydrophobic core, it is a very dynamic protein domain in the absence of a bound CID domain as previously shown by NMR measurements (Ebert et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ebert et al., 2008.

claim: CD spectra and thermal denaturations were similar for all NCBD variants.
source: CD spectra (Figure 7D–F) and thermal denaturations (Figure 7G–I) were similar for all NCBD variants.
evidence: This claim is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 7D-I.

claim: The most ancient D/P NCBD variant was slightly less stable than historically subsequent variants in the deuterostome lineage.
source: The most ancient D/P NCBD variant was slightly less stable than historically subsequent variants in the deuterostome lineage, as determined by the midpoint from far UV CD-monitored urea denaturation experiments (Figure 5D and Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by urea denaturation experiments shown in Figure 5D and Table 3.

claim: Evolution of higher affinity correlates with a somewhat reduced conformational heterogeneity in CID/NCBD complexes.
source: Comparison of the structural ensembles for the three complexes and their relative free-energy projections indicates that evolution of higher affinity correlates with a somewhat reduced conformational heterogeneity (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulations and NMR data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The ancient complex is slightly less structured and more compact, with an average helical fraction of 0.41.
source: Indeed, the free-energy surfaces as a function of the fraction of the overall helix-content and the radius of gyration (Rg) show that the ancient complex is slightly less structured and more compact, with an average helical fraction of 0.41.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulations using NMR chemical shifts as restraints.

claim: The 1R/2R complex has an average helical fraction of 0.44.
source: The younger 1R/2R complex is a little more structured in particular with respect to the C-terminal helix of NCBD, with an average helical fraction of 0.44.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulations using NMR chemical shifts as restraints.

claim: The extant human complex has an average helical fraction of 0.47.
source: The extant human complex, finally, is again slightly more structured at the N- and C- terminal helices of CID, with an average helical fraction of 0.47.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulations using NMR chemical shifts as restraints.

claim: The most ancient complex appears to have more but less populated contacts than younger complexes.
source: Indeed, the most ancient complex appears to have more but less populated contacts than younger complexes, in line with a marginally more disordered interface (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by contact analysis from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 10.

claim: During evolution, the total number of possible contacts between the domains decreases while the average population of the formed contacts increases.
source: During evolution, the total number of possible contacts between the domains decreases while the average population of the formed contacts increases.
evidence: This claim is supported by contact analysis from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 10.

claim: The A2106Q mutation did not change the affinity for NCOA2 CID.
source: The A2106Q mutation did not change the affinity for NCOA2 CID.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: The Y2108Q and the double mutation A2106Q/Y2108Q resulted in a slightly lower affinity (twofold) toward NCOA2 CID.
source: The Y2108Q and the double mutation A2106Q/Y2108Q resulted in a slightly lower affinity (twofold) toward NCOA2 CID (Table 1), in support of the simulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in Table 1.

claim: The interaction between two disordered proteins has emerged from a low-affinity complex.
source: We have used evolutionary biochemistry to reconstruct the evolutionary process by which the interaction between two disordered proteins has emerged from a low-affinity complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined phylogenetic, biophysical, and computational data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A combination of direct interactions and structural heterogeneity contributed to optimizing the affinity of the CID/NCBD complex.
source: By identifying and resurrecting the early ancestor partners, we show how a combination of direct interactions and structural heterogeneity contributed to optimizing the affinity of the CID/NCBD complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined biophysical and computational data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a remarkably high tolerance to mutation in the interface of the CID/NCBD protein-protein interaction in extant complexes.
source: In accordance, we observe a remarkably high tolerance to mutation in the interface of this particular protein-protein interaction in extant complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments showing similar affinities despite sequence variations.

claim: The initial native contacts formed during the binding reaction between human NCOA3 CID (ACTR) and CREBBP NCBD are made between residues in the respective α1 of the two domains.
source: We have previously shown that the initial native contacts formed during the binding reaction between human NCOA3 CID (ACTR) and CREBBP NCBD are made between residues in the respective α1 of the two domains (Iešmantavičius et al., 2014; Dogan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Iešmantavičius et al., 2014 and Dogan et al., 2013.

claim: Both Cα1 and Nα1 contain leucine-rich motifs, which are very common in protein-protein interactions.
source: Both Cα1 and Nα1 contain leucine-rich motifs, which are very common in protein-protein interactions (Kobe and Deisenhofer, 1994) and which are conserved in the CID/NCBD interaction (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and a citation to Kobe and Deisenhofer, 1994.

claim: Leucine-rich motifs in Cα1 and Nα1 are conserved in the CID/NCBD interaction.
source: Both Cα1 and Nα1 contain leucine-rich motifs, which are very common in protein-protein interactions (Kobe and Deisenhofer, 1994) and which are conserved in the CID/NCBD interaction (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2.

claim: Extant fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) NCBD has a low affinity for the human CID domains.
source: In contrast, in extant fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), a proteostome, the NCBD domain is preserved but, similarly to D/P NCBD it has a low affinity for the human CID domains (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in Table 1.

claim: The leucine-rich motif in Cα1 is mutated in fruit fly NCBD.
source: The leucine-rich motif in Cα1 is mutated in fruit fly NCBD (Figure 2) and the C-terminal region is more similar to D/P NCBD.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2.

claim: The affinity of the extant human PNT domain of ETS-2 is similar for ancient and extant NCBD domains (∼1 µM).
source: With these observations in mind, we note that the affinity of the extant human PNT domain of ETS-2 is similar for ancient and extant NCBD domains (∼1 µM, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding experiments reported in Table 1.

claim: The PNT/NCBD interaction was present before, and preserved during the evolution of the CID/NCBD interaction.
source: Although we have not resurrected the ancient versions of the PNT domain, these results suggest that the PNT/NCBD interaction was present before, and preserved during the evolution of the CID/NCBD interaction.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from binding affinity data and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The PNT domain is present in protostomes (e.g. D. melanogaster), while the CID domain is not.
source: Consistently, the PNT domain is present in protostomes (e.g. D. melanogaster), while the CID domain is not.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: NCBD employs distinct residues for the interaction with IRF-3, which allows this interaction to coexist with those of CID and p53TAD.
source: On a residue level, it is clear that NCBD employs distinct residues for the interaction with IRF-3, which allows this interaction (and the alternative conformation of NCBD) to coexist with those of CID and p53TAD (Figure 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by contact analysis from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 11.

claim: For CID and p53TAD, similar residues have been used throughout evolution for interactions, albeit with different relative influences.
source: For CID and p53TAD, similar residues have been used throughout evolution for interactions, albeit with different relative influences.
evidence: This claim is supported by contact analysis from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 11.

claim: In the complex between CREBBP NCBD and IRF-3, NCBD adopts a completely different conformation as compared to the conformation with CID domains and p53TAD.
source: Intriguingly, in the complex between CREBBP NCBD and IRF-3 (Qin et al., 2005), NCBD adopts a completely different conformation as compared to the conformation with CID domains and p53TAD (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Qin et al., 2005 and Lee et al., 2010.

claim: NMR and folding experiments suggest that NCBD can adopt two different conformations in absence of ligand.
source: Furthermore, NMR and folding experiments suggest that NCBD can adopt two different conformations in absence of ligand, one of which is the CID-bound conformation and the other possibly the IRF-3 bound conformation, although this has not been experimentally confirmed (Kjaergaard et al., 2010a, 2013; Dogan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kjaergaard et al., 2010a, 2013 and Dogan et al., 2016.

claim: The interaction between NCBD from CREBBP and CID from NCOA3 (ACTR) represents a classical example of coupled folding and binding of disordered protein domains.
source: The interaction between CID from NCOA3 (ACTR) and NCBD from CREBBP represents a classical example of coupled folding and binding of disordered protein domains (Demarest et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Demarest et al., 2002.

claim: NCBD is a molten-globule-like domain.
source: This interaction involves disordered protein domains from two different transcriptional coactivators: (i) the molten-globule-like (Kjaergaard et al., 2010a) nuclear co-activator binding domain (NCBD) present in the two paralogs CREB-binding protein (CREBBP, also known as CBP) and p300
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kjaergaard et al., 2010a.

claim: CID is a highly disordered domain.
source: and (ii) the highly disordered CREBBP-interacting domain (CID), found in the three mammalian paralogs NCOA1, 2 and 3 (also called SRC1, TIF2 and ACTR, respectively).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about CID that is consistent with CD data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The amino acid substitution rates in NCOA and CREBBP/p300 are higher for all domains during the early times of animal evolution and up to the common ancestor of fish and tetrapods 390 Myr ago.
source: In general, the amino acid substitution rates in NCOA and CREBBP/p300 are higher for all domains during the early times of animal evolution and up to the common ancestor of fish and tetrapods 390 Myr ago.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Within CREBBP, the substitution rate of NCBD is similar to those of the ordered histone acetyltransferase (HAT) and RING/PHD domains.
source: Within CREBBP, the substitution rate of NCBD is similar to those of the ordered histone acetyltransferase (HAT) and RING/PHD domains, whereas KIX and TAZ1 have remained more conserved.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: KIX and TAZ1 domains have remained more conserved than NCBD, HAT, and RING/PHD.
source: Within CREBBP, the substitution rate of NCBD is similar to those of the ordered histone acetyltransferase (HAT) and RING/PHD domains, whereas KIX and TAZ1 have remained more conserved.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: For CID and NCBD, functional constraints of the domains rather than disorder per se is probably determining amino acid substitution rate.
source: Thus, for CID and NCBD, functional constraints of the domains rather than disorder per se is probably determining amino acid substitution rate, similarly to a subset of disordered regions highlighted in earlier studies (Brown et al., 2011, 2010, 2002).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the substitution rate analysis and supported by citations to Brown et al., 2011, 2010, 2002.

claim: The first α-helix (Cα1) of NCOA1 CID and NCOA3 CID occupy similar positions in their respective complexes with NCBD.
source: A structural alignment shows that the NCBD domain aligns well in the two complexes but that only the first α-helix (Cα1) of NCOA1 CID and NCOA3 CID occupy similar positions (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The third α-helix (Cα3) of NCOA1 CID aligns with the second α-helix (Cα2) of NCOA3 CID.
source: In fact, the third α-helix (Cα3) of NCOA1 CID aligns with the second α-helix (Cα2) of NCOA3 CID, while Cα2 of NCOA1 CID is non-binding and split into two smaller α-helices.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of NMR structures.

claim: Cα2 of NCOA1 CID is non-binding and split into two smaller α-helices.
source: In fact, the third α-helix (Cα3) of NCOA1 CID aligns with the second α-helix (Cα2) of NCOA3 CID, while Cα2 of NCOA1 CID is non-binding and split into two smaller α-helices.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of NMR structures.

claim: The first α-helix of NCBD (Nα1) interacts with Cα1 in both NCOA1 and NCOA3 complexes.
source: The first α-helix of NCBD (Nα1) interacts with Cα1 in both complexes, but the conformation of the third α-helix (Nα3) is slightly different in the two complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of NMR structures.

claim: The conformation of the third α-helix (Nα3) of NCBD is slightly different in the NCOA1 and NCOA3 complexes.
source: The first α-helix of NCBD (Nα1) interacts with Cα1 in both complexes, but the conformation of the third α-helix (Nα3) is slightly different in the two complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of NMR structures.

claim: Residues forming the Nα1/Cα1 interface in the CID/NCBD complex are conserved in the deuterostome lineage.
source: Residues forming the Nα1/Cα1 interface in the CID/NCBD complex are conserved in the deuterostome lineage, while Nα3 has accumulated five substitutions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nα3 of NCBD has accumulated five substitutions during evolution in the deuterostome lineage.
source: Residues forming the Nα1/Cα1 interface in the CID/NCBD complex are conserved in the deuterostome lineage, while Nα3 has accumulated five substitutions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A.
